title: 1 Chronicles 5:23–26
context: The chapter closes with the half-tribe of Manasseh east of the Jordan, which increased from Bashan to Baal Hermon, Senir, and Mount Hermon (compare Deuteronomy 3:9, where Senir is given as a name of Hermon). Its heads are honored as mighty men of valor, but the Chronicler then gives his verdict on all the eastern tribes: they trespassed against the God of their fathers and played the prostitute after the gods of the peoples whom God had destroyed before them. So the God of Israel stirred up the spirit of Pul and of Tilgath Pilneser, kings of Assyria, who carried them away to Halah, Habor, Hara, and the river of Gozan. The verse can be compared with 2 Kings 15:19, 15:29, and 17:6, which name Pul, Tiglath Pileser, and the places of deportation in somewhat different ways; Hara does not appear in 2 Kings 17:6, and the Chronicler’s account is left to stand as written. The places named are generally located in upper Mesopotamia, though precise sites are debated. Arminian and Reformed readers share the conviction that the exile was God’s just judgment on persistent unfaithfulness and that God rules over the kings of the nations. They describe the manner of God’s rule over foreign agents differently, as in other passages where God uses agents to carry out judgment (compare Judges 9:23), and both affirm that the Assyrian kings acted according to their own purposes while God accomplished his.

verses.text: The children of the half-tribe of Manasseh lived in the land. They increased from Bashan to Baal Hermon, Senir, and Mount Hermon.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the half-tribe of Manasseh lived in the land and increased from Bashan to Baal Hermon, Senir, and Mount Hermon. The verse shows growth and blessing in the inheritance God gave, which makes the turn to unfaithfulness in verse 25 all the more sobering.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the tribe’s increase as God’s gift and note the geographic markers reaching to Hermon (compare Deuteronomy 3:9). Both traditions agree that the Chronicler first records the blessing God gave the eastern tribes before describing how they turned away from him.

verses.text: These were the heads of their fathers’ houses: Epher, Ishi, Eliel, Azriel, Jeremiah, Hodaviah, and Jahdiel—mighty men of valor, famous men, heads of their fathers’ houses.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers observe that the heads of Manasseh’s fathers’ houses are named and honored as mighty men of valor and famous men. The Chronicler gives them genuine credit, showing that human strength and renown are real goods, but the next verse shows that they did not secure faithfulness to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly note the honor given these leaders and see the contrast with the following verses as a warning that renown cannot replace covenant loyalty. Both traditions agree that the Chronicler sets fame and valor beside unfaithfulness to show that the people’s standing before God depended on trust and obedience.

verses.text: They trespassed against the God of their fathers, and played the prostitute after the gods of the peoples of the land whom God destroyed before them.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see in this verse the real moral responsibility of the eastern tribes, who trespassed against the God of their fathers and played the prostitute after the gods of the peoples whom God had destroyed before them. The language of unfaithfulness in marriage portrays covenant betrayal as a personal turning away from the God who had shown them kindness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise emphasize the gravity of the tribes’ sin and the covenant language of unfaithfulness. Both traditions agree that the verse explains the exile as judgment on persistent idolatry, and that the irony is sharp: Israel turned to the gods of peoples whom God himself had removed before them.

verses.text: So the God of Israel stirred up the spirit of Pul king of Assyria, and the spirit of Tilgath Pilneser king of Assyria, and he carried away the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, and brought them to Halah, Habor, Hara, and to the river of Gozan, to this day.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers affirm that the God of Israel stirred up the spirit of the Assyrian kings to carry the eastern tribes into exile. They commonly understand God’s action as directing and using the ambitions these kings already pursued, giving the tribes over to the consequences of their unfaithfulness. As in Judges 9:23, God works justly through agents who act from their own motives, and the Assyrian kings remain responsible for what they did.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers affirm the same text and commonly read it as showing that God ordained and governed the Assyrian conquest, so that the kings’ own designs served his righteous judgment, as in Judges 9:23. Both traditions agree that God is not the author of sin, that the exile was just, and that the kings acted willingly. Interpreters differ on whether Pul is another name for the same king (compare 2 Kings 15:19, 29), and the places listed differ from 2 Kings 17:6, which the Chronicler leaves unharmonized.
